summary.text: The Vine–Matthews–Morley hypothesis says that ocean crust records flips in the direction of Earth's magnetic field as the seafloor spreads.
New crust at a mid-ocean ridge locks in the field's direction as it cools, then moves away equally on both sides, so matching bands of normal and reversed magnetism lie on either side of the ridge.
It was the first key scientific test of seafloor spreading, and its main impact was letting scientists work out how fast plates move apart at mid-ocean ridges.

facts.label: Key impact
facts.value: Plate motion rates at ridges could be computed

items.prompt: A ship tows a magnetometer in a straight line across a mid-ocean ridge. What pattern should the readings show?

options.label: One steady reading the whole way across
Readings that climb steadily away from the crest
Highs and lows that mirror each other across the crest
Random jumps with no order on either side

items.explain: Crust forms symmetrically at the ridge and records normal or reversed magnetism, so the towed magnetometer picks up high and low anomalies that match on both sides.

items.prompt: Molten rock pours out at a ridge but does not yet hold any record of Earth's magnetic field. What has to happen before it can?

options.label: It must sink back into the deep mantle
It must cool below a certain temperature
It must soak up minerals from seawater
It must be buried under thick sediment

items.explain: Only after the magma cools through the Curie point do its magnetic minerals line up with the field, and once fully cooled that direction is locked in.

items.prompt: Two strips of seafloor, each 50 km from a ridge crest but on opposite sides, carry the same magnetic direction. What best explains the match?

options.label: They formed together at the crest and moved apart equally
Seawater magnetized both strips at the very same time
Both lie at the same depth below the ocean surface
Lightning struck both strips during a single storm

items.explain: New crust is made continuously and symmetrically at the ridge, and older crust moves away equally on each side, so strips of the same age sit at the same distance on both flanks.

items.prompt: What did the hypothesis let scientists calculate at mid-ocean ridges?

options.label: How deep the ocean will be in future
When the next large earthquake will hit
How much oil lies under the seabed
How fast the plates there move apart

items.explain: Its key impact was that rates of plate motion at mid-ocean ridges could be computed from the magnetic record.

items.prompt: When the idea first appeared, why were some scientists doubtful of it?

options.label: It rested on several ideas not yet widely accepted
Its authors refused to share their ship data
It contradicted measurements of lava on land
Nobody had yet towed a magnetometer at sea

items.explain: It assumed seafloor spreading, geomagnetic reversals and remanent magnetism, all hypotheses that were still not widely accepted at the time.

items.prompt: By combining land and seafloor data, how far back does the accurate record of magnetic field reversals now reach?

options.label: About 2,000 years
About 700,000 years
Almost 200 million years
Nearly 4 billion years

items.explain: Early work covered only about the last 700,000 years, but later drilling and marine surveys joined with land data gave an accurate time scale for almost 200 million years.
